title: B+trees
goal: By the end, you can explain why a database index is a short, wide tree of pages, follow an insert that splits a page and grows the tree at the top, read a real PostgreSQL index page by page, and build a small B+tree that finds one key or a whole range.
opening:
Picture a café owner on the phone to the payments company. A customer says she paid twice for one coffee and reads out the payment number from her receipt. The support person types it in, and the screen thinks. Behind it, a program reads all million payments to find one.

The tempting fix comes from a first programming course: keep the numbers sorted and halve the search at every step, as binary search does. That's fast in memory. On disk, each step reads another 8 KB page, and the steps add up. Smart people reach for it because it's the textbook answer, and the textbook was thinking of memory.

In The buffer pool, we kept busy pages in memory, but nothing says which page holds a given payment. In this lesson, we'll build a tree so short and wide that a million rows sit three page reads away. We'll watch it split and grow, read a real one, and meet a version that never overwrites a page. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments table from the opening holds 1,000,000 payments. PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run, keeps an index on the payment number: a B-tree, the structure this lesson builds. About how many pages of that index does it read to find payment 424242?
options: About 20, one for each step of halving the search
1, because the index jumps straight to the payment
All 2,745 pages of the index, because they're small and quick to read
warmup.why: Each index page holds a few hundred payment numbers, so each step down the tree narrows the search a few hundred times, not 2 times. Three steps cover a million payments, and a lookup reads one page per step. The first Try it shows `Buffers: shared hit=4`: three index pages, then the table page that holds the row. Twenty is what a tree with one number per page would need. Another kind of index, a hash index, can jump almost straight to a key, but a B-tree always walks down from the top.

sections.h: Finding one payment in a million needs a short, wide tree
sections.body:
The table from the opening lives in PostgreSQL, which stores a table as a file of pages: blocks of 8 KB that it always reads and writes whole. Our `payments` table has a million rows, one per payment, in 6,400 pages. It's a heap, the kind of table file from Pages, tuples and heap files: each new row goes wherever there's room, in no order.

So PostgreSQL has one way to find payment 424242: read every page and check every row. In the first Try it, that takes about 24 ms. That sounds quick until support staff and shop owners ask 2,000 such questions a second. At 24 ms each, that's 48 seconds of reading for every second that passes.

We want an index: a separate structure that takes a key, the value we look a row up by, and says where the row is. The store in Bytes, pages and durability: a log-structured store kept its index in memory, as a hash map that jumps from each key to its value. That needs every key in memory at once. And a hash map keeps no order, so it can't answer "every payment from 1,000 to 1,999". We want the keys sorted, on disk.

Version 1 is a sorted list in a file: pairs of a payment number and the row's address. About 400 pairs fit in a page, so a million take 2,500 pages. To find one, use binary search: look at the middle, keep the half that could hold the number, and repeat. That's about 12 page reads, each at a different spot in the file. Tolerable. Inserting isn't. A new number in the middle pushes every pair after it along by one, which rewrites half the file: 1,250 pages for one insert.

Version 2 is the binary search tree, stored on disk. Each node holds one key and two pointers, to smaller and bigger keys, and an insert adds one node. Even kept balanced, with no branch longer than the rest, a tree of a million keys is 20 levels deep. That's 20 page reads per lookup, each somewhere else, and each 8 KB page holds a single 8-byte key.

A library shows the way out. Nobody searches its thousands of shelves one by one. A board by the door says which floor holds which shelf numbers, a sign on each floor says which aisle, and each shelf keeps its books in order. You read three signs, however big the library is.

Version 3 does the same with pages. Each node is one page: a sorted list of a few hundred keys, with the page number of a child next to each. Every step down now divides the search by a few hundred instead of by 2. With 400 children per node, one level covers 400 keys, two levels 160,000, and three levels 64 million. That's the **B-tree**, published by Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight in 1970. Its variant, the B+tree, is the default index in PostgreSQL and in two other widely used databases, Oracle and MySQL.

The figure shows a toy B+tree whose nodes hold at most 3 keys. Its top node, the root, is the board by the door, the middle nodes are the floor signs, and the bottom nodes, the leaves, are the shelves.

In the Try it, PostgreSQL's index on a million rows is 3 levels deep. A lookup reads 4 pages: one per level, then the table page with the row. The top two levels are only 11 pages, and every lookup passes through them. So their usage counts (The buffer pool's tally of recent use) stay high, and the clock sweep that picks pages to throw out passes them by. On a busy database, a lookup usually reads at most two pages from disk: the leaf and the table page. Next, we'll look inside the two kinds of node.

aside.title: Why not a hash table, which jumps straight to a key?
aside.body: A hash table runs each key through a hash function, a formula that scrambles it into a slot number, and jumps to that slot. PostgreSQL does offer hash indexes, and they answer "is this exact key here?" well. But the scrambling throws the order away. A hash index can't find a range of keys, can't hand back rows in sorted order, and can't cover two columns. A B+tree does all of that at a cost of three or four page reads, which is why it's the default.

try.title: One row out of a million
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers, so nothing gets installed on your computer. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's window for typing commands, with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.

Paste the first part. Commands to a database are written in SQL, the language most databases understand. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` makes a `payments` table of a million rows, numbered by `generate_series`, with no index. `SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0` stops PostgreSQL from sharing the work among helper processes, so the counts are easy to read. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE ...)` runs a query and reports what PostgreSQL did. Predict its `Buffers` line, the count of pages it touched.
Add the primary key, which builds a B-tree index on `id`, and run the same query twice. Predict how many pages it reads now.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
The table has 6,400 pages, and without an index the query reads all of them. `hit` counts pages that were already in PostgreSQL's own memory, its buffer pool, and `read` counts pages it had to fetch from the operating system:

```text
 Seq Scan on payments (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (id = 424242)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 999999
   Buffers: shared hit=2304 read=4096
 ...
 Execution Time: 23.974 ms
```

With the primary key, the same query reads 4 pages, and the second run finds all of them in memory:

```text
 Index Scan using payments_pkey on payments (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (id = 424242)
   Index Searches: 1
   Buffers: shared hit=4
 ...
 Execution Time: 0.031 ms
```

(output trimmed). Three of the 4 pages are the index's three levels, and one is the table page with the row. The whole index is 2,745 pages, and the lookup reads 3 of them. `ALTER TABLE ... ADD PRIMARY KEY` builds the index by sorting all the keys and filling leaves from left to right, which is faster than a million inserts. Your timings will differ.

sections.h: Inside the tree: signposts on top, every key at the bottom
sections.body:
The figure has two kinds of node.

A **leaf** is a node on the bottom level. It holds keys with their values, in key order. In a PostgreSQL index, the value is the row's ctid, its address in the table: a page number and a slot on that page, from Pages, tuples and heap files. Each leaf also holds the page number of its right neighbour. Walk sideways along the bottom, and you read every key in order, like walking along the shelves.

An **internal node** is any node above the leaves. It holds only signposts, called **separator keys**, and the page numbers of its children. A node with n separators has n + 1 children, and the separators say which child covers which keys. The node `30 50` sends keys below 30 to its first child, 30 to 49 to its second, and 50 or more to its third.

Let's find 60 in the figure. At the root, 60 is below 70, so go left. In `30 50`, 60 is at least 50, so take the third child. That leaf holds `50 60`, and there's our key. One page per level: three reads.

That's a B+tree. Bayer and McCreight's original B-tree also kept values in internal nodes, so some searches could stop halfway down. Moving every value into the leaves gives up that shortcut and buys two things. Internal nodes hold only keys and page numbers, so more of them fit in a page. The tree gets wider and shorter, and its top is small enough to stay in memory. And every key sits in a linked leaf, so a range is one walk along the bottom, as the fourth section shows.

The toy tree has **order 4**: a node has at most 4 children, so at most 3 keys. Books define "order" in different ways; this lesson and its lab use this one. A real page is far wider. A PostgreSQL index entry for an `int` key, a whole number of 4 bytes, takes 20 bytes. That's an 8-byte header holding the row's ctid, the key padded to 8 bytes, and a 4-byte line pointer: the slot at the front of the page that points to the entry. The page also spends 24 bytes on its own header and 16 at its end, where it keeps the links to its neighbours. So (8,192 - 24 - 16) / 20 = 407 entries fit.

The number of children per node is the **fanout**. With a fanout in the hundreds, an index stays at 3 or 4 levels for any table you're likely to meet.

The Try it shows two more details. Page 0 of every index is a metapage, a page of notes that says which page is the root. And every page except the rightmost on its level starts with a **high key**, an upper limit for the keys allowed on that page. It helps when many queries run at once. A search may land on a page that another query split a moment ago, so its key has moved to the right neighbour. The high key tells it so, and it follows the link. That design comes from Philip Lehman and S. Bing Yao, in 1981.

Next, we'll fill a page and see what the tree does.

try.title: Read the pages of a real index
steps: In the same psql window, ask the metapage where the root is. `bt_metap` and the other functions here come from pageinspect, an add-on (PostgreSQL calls it an extension) that shows the raw contents of pages; the lab database has it switched on. `level` counts the levels below the root, so 0 would mean the root is itself a leaf.
List the root's first items. `ctid` holds each child's page number, and `data` holds the separator key as raw bytes, smallest byte first. Predict how many children the root has.
Look at page 1, the leftmost leaf. Then count the pages of the whole index by type: `l` for leaf, `i` for internal and `r` for root.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
 root | level
------+-------
  290 |     2

 itemoffset |  ctid   |          data
------------+---------+-------------------------
          1 | (3,0)   |
          2 | (289,1) | 09 96 01 00 00 00 00 00
          3 | (575,1) | 11 2c 03 00 00 00 00 00

 blkno | type | live_items | free_size | btpo_next
-------+------+------------+-----------+-----------
     1 | l    |        367 |       808 |         2

 itemoffset | ctid  |          data
------------+-------+-------------------------
          1 | (2,1) | 6f 01 00 00 00 00 00 00
          2 | (0,1) | 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
          3 | (0,2) | 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

 type | pages | avg_items
------+-------+-----------
 i    |    10 |       274
 l    |  2733 |       367
 r    |     1 |        10
```

The root is page 290, and level 2 means two levels below it: three in all. In the root, the page number in `ctid` is the link down to a child. The first item has no key, so it covers everything below the second item's key. That key is `09 96 01 00` read smallest byte first: 0x019609, which is 103,945. So page 289 starts at payment 103,945. Leaf 1 holds 367 items and links to leaf 2. Its first item is the high key, 367 (`6f 01`), which is the first key of leaf 2. Then come the entries: key 1 points at row (0,1), slot 1 on page 0 of the table. So 2,733 leaves of 367 keys hold the million rows. 367 is 90% of the 407 that would fit, because PostgreSQL builds an index with its leaves 90% full by default, leaving room for later inserts.

sections.h: A full page splits, and the tree grows at the top
sections.body:
An insert starts as a search. Walk down to the leaf where the new key belongs and add it there, in order. Usually it fits, and the insert changes one page.

Sometimes the leaf is full. Version 1 would make the page bigger, but a page has a fixed size, which is the whole point of pages. Version 2 would chain an extra page, an overflow page, to the full leaf. Every key that lands there then piles into the chain, which must be read page by page. That's the slow search we built the tree to escape.

Version 3 is the **split**, and the stepper below walks through one. The full leaf gets a new neighbour on its right, and the upper half of its keys moves there. The parent, the node one level up, now needs the new leaf's page number and a separator that says where the new leaf starts. The separator is the new leaf's first key, and it's **copied** up: it stays in the leaf too, because the leaves must hold every key.

The parent may be full as well. Then it splits the same way, with one difference: its middle key is **pushed** up and leaves both halves, because keys in internal nodes are only signposts. Splits can climb all the way to the root. When the root splits, a new root with a single key is made above it. That's the only way a B+tree gets taller, so every leaf is always at the same depth, and every search reads the same number of pages.

Here the library picture breaks. A library grows at its edges, with a new wing. A B+tree grows by putting a new sign above the board at the door, so every shelf stays the same number of signs from the entrance.

A split leaves two half-full pages behind. When keys arrive in random order, pages refill unevenly, and the index settles at about two-thirds full: 64% to 67% in our runs of the Try it. PostgreSQL treats one case specially. When the page that splits is the rightmost leaf, as it is when every new key is bigger than the last, it keeps the left page 90% full. That 90% is the B-tree's default `fillfactor`: how full PostgreSQL packs a page, leaving the rest free.

The kind of key decides which case you get. A UUID is a 16-byte id, usually written as 32 digits and letters from a to f, that any computer can make on its own with almost no chance of a clash. The classic kind, from `gen_random_uuid()`, is random. PostgreSQL 18 added `uuidv7()`, whose ids start with the current time, so each new one is bigger than the last. In one run of the Try it, 200,000 random UUIDs took 1,038 leaf pages, and 200,000 time-ordered ones took 767. That's a third more pages for the same rows, and every random insert needs a different leaf in memory.

A split also costs writes. It changes the old leaf, the new leaf and the parent, and each change first goes to the database's log, the subject of Write-ahead logging and crash recovery. Next, we'll put the linked leaves to work.

stepper.intro: Watch one insert split a leaf, then the root, and grow a new level. Click Next and Back, or use the arrow keys.

frames.say: The split makes a new leaf on the right, moves the upper half (`90 100`) into it and links it into the row of leaves. The parent needs a pointer to the new leaf and a separator for it: the new leaf's first key, 90. It's **copied** up, so 90 is still in the leaf, where every key must be. Now the root has 4 keys, one too many.

--------+------------+------------------

sections.h: Walking the leaves: ranges, and indexes on two columns
sections.body:
`WHERE id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1999` asks for every payment numbered 1,000 to 1,999. (`WHERE` is the part of an SQL query that says which rows you want.) This is where the linked leaves pay off. The index walks down once, to the leaf that holds 1,000: the same three page reads as a lookup. Then it reads along that leaf and follows the link to the next one, until it meets a key above 1,999. A thousand keys at 367 per leaf span 3 or 4 leaves, so the scan reads 6 index pages in all. A thousand separate lookups would read 3,000.

An index can also cover several columns. It sorts by the first column, then by the second within each value of the first. A library does the same when it shelves books by subject and, within each subject, by author. One author's cookery books are easy to find: go to cookery, then to the author. Everything by that author, whatever the subject, means a stop in every subject.

The Try it builds that case. A made-up table of payouts to shops has a `region` (0 to 3), a batch number, `batch_id`, and an index on `(region, batch_id)`. `WHERE region = 2 AND batch_id = 7700` is one walk down to one spot. `WHERE batch_id = 7700` alone is harder, because the matching entries sit in four places, one inside each region's run of entries. Before PostgreSQL 18, the choice was to read every leaf of the index or the whole table.

PostgreSQL 18 added **skip scan**: it walks down once per region, as if you had asked for `region = 0`, then `region = 1`, and so on. In the Try it, that costs 22 pages (`Index Searches: 6`), where reading the table costs 5,440. Skip scan only pays when the first column has few different values. With 50,000 shops in front, 50,000 walks down lose to reading the table.

The PostgreSQL docs give the rule. Exact matches on the leading columns, plus a range on the first column without one, decide how much of the index is read. **Put the exact-match columns first and the range column last.** For "this shop's payments since 1 November", it feels natural to lead with time: `(created_at, merchant_id)`. (The lab calls shops merchants.) But then one shop's entries are scattered among every other shop's, and the scan reads and throws away most of what it touches. `(merchant_id, created_at)` puts that shop's entries side by side.

One last question: what does a leaf point at? In PostgreSQL every index, the primary key's included, stores ctids, and the row itself lives in the heap. That heap page is the fourth page in the first Try it. InnoDB, the part of MySQL that stores data, keeps the whole row in the leaves of the primary key's index, so that index is the table. That's a **clustered index**. Its other indexes store the primary key instead of an address, so a lookup through one of them walks down two trees. Oracle offers both: its ordinary tables are heaps like PostgreSQL's, and an index-organized table works like InnoDB's. Indexes and reading EXPLAIN measures what each choice costs.

Every change in this lesson has overwritten pages in place. Next, we'll see what that risks, and meet a tree that never does it.

sections.h: A tree that never overwrites a page: copy-on-write
sections.body:
Look at what a split writes: the old leaf, its new neighbour and the parent, in three separate page writes. Picture the power failing between them. The file then holds half a split: a parent pointing at a page that was never written, or a new page that nothing points at. PostgreSQL, InnoDB and Oracle guard against that with a log written before any page changes, which Write-ahead logging and crash recovery builds. There's a second answer: never overwrite a page that the current tree uses.

LMDB works that way. It's a small key-value store: code that a program builds in to keep keys and their values in one file. To change a leaf, LMDB writes a changed copy of the leaf to a free page. The parent must now point at the copy, so the parent is copied too, and so on up to a new root. That's one new page per level, three for a three-level tree, as the figure shows. Every page the change didn't touch is shared by the old tree and the new one.

The commit, the moment the change counts, is one last small write. LMDB keeps two meta pages at the start of the file, each naming a root, and takes turns between them: the new root goes into the older one. Until that write lands, the old root is the database. After a crash, LMDB opens the root that the newer meta page names, and its documentation says this design needs no special recovery procedure at all.

The old tree stays whole, so it's a free snapshot, a view of the data frozen at one moment. A reader that started before the commit keeps walking root v1 and sees the old data, unchanged. Readers never wait for the writer, and the writer never waits for readers. LMDB reuses an old version's pages once no reader needs them, instead of growing the file.

The price is paid in writes and in waiting. A one-row change copies a whole path from root to leaf, where an in-place B+tree writes one leaf page and a small log record. And LMDB lets only one writer run at a time. That suits a program that mostly reads, such as a store of settings or a local cache on one machine. A payments table taking thousands of writes at once wants the in-place tree and its log.

So both trees pay for a small change with whole pages: the in-place tree rewrites a leaf for every scattered insert, and the copy-on-write tree a whole path. Next, we'll measure that cost, and build a store that turns many small scattered writes into one long one.

compare.title: Where the row lives: PostgreSQL and InnoDB

a.label: PostgreSQL
a.title: a heap table and B-tree indexes
a.src:
primary key index (B+tree)
  leaf entry: (id 424242, ctid (2694,21))
             |
             v
heap: page 2694, slot 21 -> the row

secondary index on card
  leaf entry: ('card-4242', ctid (2694,21))

lookup by id:   3 index pages + 1 heap page
lookup by card: 3 index pages + 1 heap page

b.label: InnoDB (MySQL)
b.title: the primary key's index is the table
b.src:
primary key index (B+tree) IS the table
  leaf entry: (id 424242, card, amount, ...)

secondary index on card
  leaf entry: ('card-4242', id 424242)
             |
             v
  then a second descent of the primary key

lookup by id:   3 pages, row included
lookup by card: 3 pages + 3 pages

compare.note: Both are B+trees; what differs is what a leaf holds. PostgreSQL's leaves hold the row's address, its ctid, so every index finds the row with one extra read of the table. The cost shows when an update moves a row to another page: every index then needs a new entry, unless PostgreSQL can keep the new version on the same page (the HOT update from Pages, tuples and heap files). InnoDB's primary key leaves hold the row itself, so lookups and ranges by primary key are cheaper. But every lookup through another index walks down a second tree, and a long or random primary key makes every other index bigger.

worked.title: Estimate how tall an index will be

steps.say: Start from the size of one leaf entry. For an `int` key in PostgreSQL, that's an 8-byte header holding the row's ctid (its page and slot), the 4-byte key padded to 8 bytes, and a 4-byte line pointer in the page's list of slots.

Work out the entries per page. The page loses 24 bytes to its header and 16 to the space at its end, which holds the links to its neighbours. Leaves built by `CREATE INDEX`, or filled by keys that only grow, are 90% full.
steps.code:
max per page  = (8192 - 24 - 16) / 20 = 407
per leaf (90%) = 407 x 0.9 = 366, plus the high key = 367

steps.say: Count the pages level by level, going up until one page is enough. That page is the root. Internal pages built by `CREATE INDEX` are fuller than half but not full; the Try it measured 274 child pointers in each.
steps.code:
leaves   = 1,000,000 / 366 = 2,733
internal = 2,733 / 274    = 10
root     = 1  -> 3 levels: root, internal, leaf

steps.say: Check against the real index: `bt_metap` said level 2 (three levels), and `bt_multi_page_stats` counted 2,733 leaves and 10 internal pages. The same sums in Kotlin show how slowly the height grows.

lab.title: Build a B+tree of order 4
steps: Open `BPlusTree.kt`. Read `Node`, `Leaf` and `Internal` at the top, then `childIndex` and `checkInvariants` at the bottom. The checker is the list of rules your tree must keep: keys in order, no node too full, every leaf at the same depth, and a leaf chain that visits every leaf from left to right.
Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 10 fail for now.

Write `get`: start with `read(root)`, follow `children[childIndex(keys, key)]` while the node is `Internal`, then binary-search the leaf. Always follow pointers through `read`, which counts page reads the way a disk would.

Write `insert` for leaves (add the key in order, or replace the value of a key that's already there) and `put`. Then write `splitLeaf`, which copies its separator up, and the root case in `put`: a new `Internal` root, and `height++`.
Write `splitInternal`, which pushes its middle key up, and the internal branch of `insert`.
Write `range`: walk down to the leaf where `lo` belongs, then read keys and follow `next` links until a key is above `hi`. Run the tests until all 10 pass.
hints: `ArrayList.binarySearch` returns `-(insertionPoint + 1)` for a missing key, so `-(i + 1)` is where the new key goes.

A leaf split returns `Split(right.keys[0], rightId)` and keeps that key in the right leaf. An internal split returns `keys[mid]` and removes it from both halves: the left keeps `keys[0 until mid]` and `children[0..mid]`.
Before you link the new leaf, copy the old leaf's `next` into it: `right.next = leaf.next`, then `leaf.next = rightId`.
If "a range scan descends once" fails, you're probably walking down again for each leaf, or reading the next leaf after you've already found a key above `hi`.

drill.title: Write both splits from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. For a B+tree whose nodes hold `keys`, whose leaves hold `values` and `next`, and whose internal nodes hold `children`, write `splitLeaf` and `splitInternal`. Each returns the separator for the parent and the new node's page id. Then answer: which split keeps its separator in a child, and why?

answer.src:
fun splitLeaf(leaf: Leaf): Split {
    val mid = leaf.keys.size / 2
    val right = Leaf()
    right.keys += leaf.keys.subList(mid, leaf.keys.size)
    right.values += leaf.values.subList(mid, leaf.values.size)
    leaf.keys.subList(mid, leaf.keys.size).clear()
    leaf.values.subList(mid, leaf.values.size).clear()
    right.next = leaf.next                    // splice into the leaf chain
    val id = allocate(right)
    leaf.next = id
    return Split(right.keys[0], id)           // copy up: the key stays in the leaf
}

fun splitInternal(node: Internal): Split {
    val mid = node.keys.size / 2
    val up = node.keys[mid]
    val right = Internal()
    right.keys += node.keys.subList(mid + 1, node.keys.size)
    right.children += node.children.subList(mid + 1, node.children.size)
    node.keys.subList(mid, node.keys.size).clear()
    node.children.subList(mid + 1, node.children.size).clear()
    return Split(up, allocate(right))         // push up: the key leaves both halves
}

// The leaf split keeps its separator, because the leaves must hold every key and value.
// Internal keys are only signposts, so the middle one can move up.

recap: A B+tree index is a tree of pages. Each page holds hundreds of keys, so three or four levels cover any table, and a lookup reads one page per level.
Internal nodes hold only separator keys and the page numbers of their children. Leaves hold every key with its value (in PostgreSQL, the row's address, its ctid) and link to the next leaf.
A full leaf splits and copies its new neighbour's first key up. A full internal node splits and pushes its middle key up. A root split adds a level at the top, so every leaf stays at the same depth.
Random keys leave pages about two-thirds full. Keys that only grow, such as `uuidv7()` ids, split the rightmost leaf, which PostgreSQL leaves 90% full, so the index needs a quarter fewer pages.
A range scan walks down once, then along the leaves. An index on several columns serves exact matches on its first columns plus one range, so put the range column last.

The limit: every change rewrites whole pages. An in-place tree rewrites a leaf for each scattered insert, and a copy-on-write tree such as LMDB's rewrites a whole path, in return for free snapshots and no recovery after a crash.
closing:
We started with a support call that waited while a program read a million payments to find one. With a B+tree, the same lookup reads three pages of the index and one page of the table, and a table a hundred times bigger adds one more page.

Next time you start the lab database, open the SQL track's database with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course` and type `\di+`. It lists every index with its size. Divide a size by 8 KB to get its pages, and guess how many levels it needs.

Next, we'll feed a B+tree random keys and count what every insert costs. Could a store keep its data sorted without ever changing a page in place?

quiz.q: A B+tree has about 400 children per internal node and 400 keys per leaf. About how many levels does it need for 64 million keys?
quiz.why: 400 x 400 x 400 = 64 million: the root points to 400 internal nodes, each of which points to 400 leaves of 400 keys. 26 is how many times you can halve 64 million, the height of a binary tree. Each level multiplies what the tree can hold by 400, which is why real indexes stay at 3 or 4 levels.

quiz.q: In a B+tree of order 4 (at most 3 keys per node), you insert 25 into the full leaf `10 20 30`. The leaf splits into `10 20` and `25 30`. What happens to 25?
options: It moves up to the parent and is removed from the leaf
Nothing goes up; the parent finds the new leaf by following the leaf chain
It's copied up as the separator and stays as the first key of the right leaf
20 is copied up, because it's the last key of the left leaf
quiz.why: A leaf split copies the new leaf's first key into the parent and keeps it in the leaf, because the leaves must hold every key and its value. Moving the key up and out of both halves is what an internal split does with its middle key. The leaf chain serves range scans; a search only goes down, so the parent needs the separator to find the new leaf.

quiz.q: A shop's screen lists its payments since 1 November: `WHERE merchant_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-11-01'`, where `merchant_id` is the shop. Which index lets PostgreSQL read one unbroken run of leaf entries?
options: Either: both columns are in the index
Neither: a B-tree can't use two conditions at once
quiz.why: With `merchant_id` first, all of shop 42's entries sit together, sorted by time. The scan starts at the first one on or after the date and stops at the next shop. With `created_at` first, shop 42's entries are scattered among every other shop's since that date, and the scan reads and throws most of them away. The third option is the trap: both columns being in the index isn't enough, because the order decides which entries sit side by side.

quiz.q: Two tables get 200,000 inserts each: one keyed by `uuidv7()`, the other by `gen_random_uuid()`. The random one's index has about a third more leaf pages. Why?
options: Random UUIDs are longer than time-ordered ones
Random keys split pages in the middle and leave them about two-thirds full, while growing keys split the rightmost leaf, which PostgreSQL leaves 90% full
PostgreSQL squeezes time-ordered UUIDs into less space
The random index has more levels, and each level adds pages
quiz.why: Both kinds of UUID are 16 bytes. What differs is where inserts land. Random keys hit pages all over the index, and each split leaves two half-full pages that refill unevenly, so leaves average about 66%. Time-ordered keys always go to the rightmost leaf, and when it splits, PostgreSQL keeps the left page at the 90% fillfactor. Both indexes have the same number of levels.

quiz.q: From The buffer pool: a lookup by primary key reads the root, an internal page, a leaf and a table page. On a busy server with a big table, which of these is most likely to need a read from disk?
options: The root, because it's the first page read
All four equally, because the clock sweep treats every page the same
The leaf and the table page
None: index pages are never thrown out of memory
quiz.why: Every lookup passes through the root and one of a few internal pages, so their usage counts, the buffer pool's tally of recent use, stay at or near the top value of 5, and the clock sweep keeps passing them by. There are thousands of leaves and table pages, and each one is touched rarely, so those are the pages whose count drops to 0 and that get thrown out. Index pages get no special protection; they stay because they're used.

flashcards.front: Why is a database index a tree with hundreds of keys per node, not a binary tree?
flashcards.back: Each node is a page, and each page read costs a trip to the disk. Hundreds of keys per page divide the search by hundreds at every step, so a million keys need 3 reads instead of 20.

flashcards.front: Leaf split or internal split: what happens to the separator?
flashcards.back: A leaf split copies the new leaf's first key up and keeps it in the leaf. An internal split pushes its middle key up and removes it from both halves.

flashcards.front: Why is every leaf of a B+tree at the same depth?
flashcards.back: The tree only grows when the root splits and a new root is made above it. It grows at the top, never at the bottom.

flashcards.front: Why do databases use the B+tree rather than the original B-tree?
flashcards.back: Internal nodes hold only keys and page numbers, so more fit per page and the tree is shorter. And linked leaves turn a range into one walk along the bottom level.

flashcards.front: How many `int` entries fit in a PostgreSQL B-tree page, and how full are the leaves after CREATE INDEX?
flashcards.back: 407 entries of 20 bytes. Leaves are filled to the default fillfactor of 90%, about 367 entries.

flashcards.front: Which column goes last in an index on several columns?
flashcards.back: The one you search by range, such as a date. Exact-match columns go first, so the matching entries sit side by side.

flashcards.front: How does a copy-on-write B-tree such as LMDB commit a change?
flashcards.back: It writes changed copies of the leaf and of every page above it up to a new root, then records the new root in a meta page. The old root stays whole as a snapshot.

terms.plain: A structure, separate from the table, that takes a key and says where the matching rows are, so a lookup doesn't read the whole table.
A balanced tree of pages whose upper nodes hold only signposts and whose linked leaves, at the bottom, hold every key and its value.
A leaf is a node on the bottom level, holding keys and values. An internal node is any node above, holding separator keys and child page numbers.
How many children an internal node has: hundreds per 8 KB page in a real index.
Moving half of a full node's keys to a new neighbour and adding a separator for it to the parent.
How full PostgreSQL packs B-tree leaves when it builds an index or splits the rightmost leaf: 90% by default.
An index whose leaves hold the table's rows themselves, as InnoDB's primary key index does.
A B-tree that never overwrites a page in use: a change writes new copies up to a new root, and switching to that root is the commit.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who's new to databases asks why finding one payment in a table of a million reads only 4 pages, and whether it will read 40 when the table holds 100 million. Explain how the index is built and what happens to the cost as the table grows.
explain_back.answer: The index is a B+tree, a tree whose nodes are 8 KB pages holding a few hundred keys each. The pages near the top hold signposts: keys that say which page below covers which range. The pages at the bottom, the leaves, hold every key with the address of its row. A lookup starts at the top and reads one page per level until it reaches the leaf, then reads the table page that holds the row. At a million rows the index has three levels: one root, about ten pages in the middle and about 2,700 leaves. That's three index pages and one table page. Each extra level multiplies what the tree can hold by a few hundred, so 100 million rows need one more level: about 5 page reads, not 40. And the top pages are used by every lookup, so they stay in memory, and usually only the leaf and the table page come from disk.

deeper.body:
**Many users in one tree.** A real index is read and changed by many queries at once. The textbook method is latch crabbing. A latch is a short lock on one page. A search holds the latch on a node, takes the latch on the child, and lets go of the parent once the child is safe, meaning it can't split. An insert that might split keeps latches on every page of the path that could split. PostgreSQL follows Lehman and Yao (1981) instead: a reader holds one page lock at a time, and if a split moved its key to the right neighbour, the high key tells it so and it follows the link. The nbtree README in the PostgreSQL source explains how a split is logged as one record for the split pages and a second for the parent, with a flag on the left page until the parent has its new pointer.

**Pages that never merge.** Textbooks merge or rebalance nodes that fall below half full after deletes. PostgreSQL's README calls merging partly full pages impractical, so it only deletes a page once the page is completely empty. An index that lost most of its rows stays big until `REINDEX` rebuilds it, or `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a database in use.

**Repeated keys and dead entries.** Since PostgreSQL 13, a leaf stores many equal keys as one key with a list of row addresses (deduplication, on by default), which shrinks indexes on columns like `status`. Since PostgreSQL 14, bottom-up index deletion removes entries that point at dead row versions right before a page would split, so a table with many updates splits less.

**Building from the bottom up.** `CREATE INDEX` on a full table doesn't insert row by row. It sorts all the keys, writes leaves left to right at the fillfactor, then builds each level above from the first key of each page below. That's why a freshly built index is dense and quick to make.

**Tables as trees, and an old idea.** SQLite, a small database built into many phone apps, stores each table itself as a B+tree: a 64-bit whole-number key per row, with all the data in the leaves. And skip scan is new to PostgreSQL, not to databases: Oracle has had it since version 9i, over twenty years ago.

**Hot pages on many machines.** Growing keys have their own cost when several database machines share one index, as in Oracle RAC: every machine inserts into the same rightmost page, and that page becomes a queue. Oracle's reverse key indexes store each key's bytes backwards to spread the inserts out, at the cost of losing range scans.
